label: Intrinsic Analysis on Manifolds
notes: This chapter, printed pages 57 to 76, builds statistics that live inside the manifold itself. Instead of embedding the data in Euclidean space, we measure with the Riemannian geodesic distance and define a mean by minimizing squared geodesic spread, the central object for everything that follows on these curved sample spaces.

label: Geodesic Distance
notes: The geodesic distance is the length of the shortest curve joining two points on the manifold, obtained by integrating the Riemannian speed along candidate paths. It respects the curved geometry, unlike the ambient chord. Every intrinsic estimator here is built from this distance, so its locality and cut-locus behaviour matter.

label: The Intrinsic Frechet Mean
notes: The intrinsic Frechet or Karcher mean minimizes the expected squared geodesic distance to a random point. It generalizes the Euclidean average, where squared distance recovers the ordinary mean. On a curved space the minimizer need not be unique, so existence and uniqueness require the careful hypotheses we develop in the slides that follow.

label: Exponential and Logarithm Maps
notes: The exponential map shoots a geodesic from a base point along a tangent vector for unit time, while the logarithm map inverts it, recording the initial velocity that reaches a target. Together they pass data between the flat tangent space and the curved manifold, the engine of every intrinsic computation in this chapter.

label: Tangent-Space Linearization
notes: At the mean, the logarithm map sends each sample to a tangent vector whose length equals its geodesic distance. Because tangent vectors add like ordinary vectors, statistics that are hard on the manifold become linear algebra in normal coordinates centered at the Karcher mean, which is exactly what makes intrinsic inference tractable.

label: Existence and Uniqueness
notes: Karcher, Kendall, Le, and Afsari give sufficient conditions: if the support lies in a regular geodesic ball whose radius is bounded by the injectivity radius and the inverse square root of the curvature, the squared distance stays convex and the intrinsic mean exists and is unique within that ball.

label: When Uniqueness Fails
notes: Spread out the data and uniqueness breaks. The uniform distribution on a sphere has every point as a Frechet minimizer, and an antipodal pair has a whole equatorial circle of means. The cut locus and positive curvature are what destroy the convexity that small regular balls otherwise enjoy.

label: The Karcher Mean Iteration
notes: We compute the mean by a tangent-space fixed point. Lift every sample through the logarithm at the current estimate, average those tangent vectors, then push the average back with the exponential map. Repeating drives the tangent average to zero, which is the first-order optimality condition for the Karcher mean.

label: Gradient and Newton Steps
notes: The averaged log vectors are exactly the negative gradient of the Frechet functional, so the iteration is Riemannian gradient descent. Replacing the step with the Hessian of the squared distance, which carries curvature corrections, yields a Newton method that converges quadratically near the mean rather than merely linearly.

label: Central Limit Theorem
notes: In normal coordinates at the population mean, the sample Karcher mean is asymptotically normal. Root-n times its coordinate vector converges to a Gaussian whose covariance is a sandwich involving the Hessian of the Frechet functional, enabling confidence regions and bootstrap two-sample tests directly in the tangent chart.

label: Intrinsic versus Extrinsic
notes: Extrinsic analysis embeds the manifold and projects the ambient mean back, which is fast and always unique. Intrinsic analysis uses the true geodesic metric and is coordinate free but costs iteration and needs concentration. The two often agree closely for tight data and diverge as the spread of the sample grows.

label: Recap and Lab
notes: We defined the geodesic distance, the Karcher mean, the exponential and logarithm maps, the regular-ball conditions, the tangent-space iteration, and the central limit theorem. The lab asks what breaks if geodesic distance is replaced by Euclidean distance, exposing why intrinsic geometry is structural and not decorative.
